paras: The lynching of Mary Sullivan was the hanging of a woman by a mob of about fifty men in Caldwell County, Kentucky, in early October 1882, after she was taken at night from a house near Dalton in neighboring Hopkins County. She had been accused of a part in the hanging of Crockett Jenkins, a member of the Campbell gang, and released, and no clue to her killers was reported. Papers across the country retold her story as that of a "female desperado," while two Kentucky papers objected to the mob hanging of a woman.

According to a Louisville dispatch, the Campbell gang was a band of Caldwell County "outlaws, murderers and robbers," three of whose members had been hanged by a mob some weeks earlier. Crockett Jenkins, another member, was then found hanged near Princeton. Mary Sullivan and Jane Sullivan, said to be intimate with the robbers, were arrested and tried at Princeton on suspicion of a part in his death, and were released for lack of evidence.

The Crittenden Press described Sullivan as Jenkins's mistress and said she had mortgaged two milch cows to pay guards while under arrest. The Louisville Commercial said that Jenkins had left her for another woman and that she had found notices warning her to leave the neighborhood after her discharge.

On a Friday night, on her way to Princeton to redeem the cows, Sullivan stopped for the night at the house of Norman Hubbard near Dalton in Hopkins County, close to the Caldwell line. About fifty men rode up to the house, called her out, and took her across the county line into Caldwell County. According to the Crittenden Press, the mob posted notices that at a later date "all the Sullivans and Campbells" in the country would be hanged.

The Commercial's account said five armed men seized her at the door, bound her, laid her across a horse and joined a mob waiting on the road. They hanged her from the same limb of the oak from which Jenkins had been hanged. Her body was found on Sunday morning a few miles from Shady Grove, with a basket of her clothing and $40 in gold nearby, and was cut down and buried at Shady Grove.

The Louisville dispatch said there was "no clue to the perpetrators," and the Madisonville Times could not learn whether the men were masked. That paper did not know whether they were the Regulators who had hanged the Campbells or friends of the gang avenging Jenkins. No report of an inquest, arrest or trial appears in the coverage.

The first notice was a Louisville dispatch carried under "Lynch Law in Kentucky" and rewritten in West Virginia as "Wholesale Lynching in Kentucky," which said the gang was "being rapidly decimated by the outraged people." The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian called it the fourth hanging to result from "the lawless state of affairs" in Caldwell County. The Crittenden Press called her Jenkins's "female partner in crime" and quoted a former neighbor who said the clan had received "the severest blow yet."

Local papers also voiced unease: the Madisonville Times said she "bore a bad, unenviable reputation" yet found it horrible that a woman was "hung like a dog." The Hartford Herald called the mob hanging of a woman murder, though it allowed that excitement over Jenkins's death offered "some sort of excuse" in Sullivan's case.

A long Louisville Commercial special, a tale of "lawless love and lawless hate," ran in Washington, St. Paul and South Carolina under headlines such as "MARY SULLIVAN'S CRIMES," "A FEMALE DESPERADO" and "A FEMALE JESSE JAMES." None of the reports stated her race.

The wire dispatch, the Crittenden Press and the Madisonville Times place the hanging on the Friday night before their reports of 9-13 October, while the Commercial dates it 29 September. The Crittenden Press put the mob's arrival at about 8 o'clock, the others at about 10. The Madisonville Times, relying on talk in the Dalton district, said she was supposed to have been hanged at a school house in Caldwell County, while the Crittenden Press reported the body found on the Jenkins tree.

She was hanged by a mob of about fifty men acting without legal authority (A1, A3, A5), after she had been accused of a part in the death of Crockett Jenkins and released for lack of evidence (A1, A5, A9).

A Louisville wire dispatch (A1), the Crittenden Press via the Memphis Public Ledger (A3, A4), the Madisonville Times (A5) and the Louisville Commercial (A8, A9) independently report the seizure and hanging, though they differ on date and details.

accounts.label: Madisonville Times (Hopkins county)

accounts.label: Louisville Commercial special
accounts.gist: On 29 September five armed men seized her at the door, bound her, carried her to a waiting mob, and hanged her from the limb where Jenkins had hung; her five-year-old child was with her at the house.

framing.detail: The wire dispatch under 'Lynch Law in Kentucky' called the Campbells 'outlaws, murderers and robbers' and reported the hanging without comment.

The Crittenden Press called her Jenkins's 'female partner in crime' and quoted a neighbor that the clan had 'received the severest blow yet.'

The Louisville Commercial story ('MARY SULLIVAN'S CRIMES', 'A FEMALE DESPERADO', 'A FEMALE JESSE JAMES') told a sensational tale of 'lawless love and lawless hate' while narrating the hanging sympathetically.
The Hartford Herald called the mob hanging of a woman 'murder', though it allowed that Sullivan's case had some excuse in excitement over Jenkins's death.
